name: Hair removal via topical hair-removal sprays

lead: Hair-removal sprays leave skin smooth quickly and painlessly, with the result visible straight away and lasting hours to days. They are a chemical depilatory, in the same family as creams, gels, lotions and roll-ons, with brands including Nair, Magic Shave and Veet.

Active ingredients are salts of thioglycolic or thiolactic acid, which break the disulfide bonds in keratin so hair can be wiped away. A typical product uses about 5-6% calcium thioglycolate with an alkaline base near pH 12, and breakdown takes about 10 minutes. The root stays in place, so hair regrows.

paras: The spray is applied to the skin, left for the time on the pack, and wiped away with the hair. Patch-test directions are included, and it is repeated whenever hair returns.
The high pH and thiol chemistry can irritate or burn skin. General hair-removal risks such as irritation and burns apply, and the dermal papilla is not destroyed, so results are temporary.

angle.text: Spray-on depilatories such as Nair or Veet dissolve hair at the skin surface so it wipes away, leaving smooth skin quickly and painlessly. The smoothness is visible immediately and lasts hours to days.

lead: Topical hair-removal sprays are aerosol or pump-applied chemical depilatories. Depilatories as a class come as gels, creams, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders, and brands include Nair, Magic Shave and Veet.[1]

They work by breaking the disulfide bonds in keratin with thioglycolate or thiolactate salts, so the hair is hydrolysed at the skin surface and wiped away.[1][2] Because the dermal papilla is not destroyed, hair regrows; effects last hours to days.[1][2] No clinical trials of spray formats specifically were found.

paras: Thioglycolic acid reacts with cystine in keratin, converting it to dithiodiglycolic acid and cysteine and weakening the hair. A typical product contains 5-6% calcium thioglycolate in a cream base with calcium or strontium hydroxide holding the pH near 12. After roughly 10 minutes the area is rinsed and conditioners restore skin pH.[1]
Chemical depilatories dissolve hair at the surface, unlike waxing and sugaring, which remove hair from the root with results lasting days to weeks.[2]

Older products used sulfides such as strontium sulfide, replaced by thiols because of their odour. Greek and Roman writers described depilatory ointments and plasters called psilothrum.[1] Wikipedia's hair-removal article also lists a 9th-century claim, marked as needing citation, that Ziryab introduced chemical depilatories in Al-Andalus.[2]

Hair-removal methods in general are associated with skin inflammation, minor burns, lesions, scarring, ingrown hairs and folliculitis.[2] A 2021 Cochrane review found hair-removal cream was associated with lower surgical-site infection risk than razors in pre-surgical settings.[2]
Chemical depilatories are described as indicated for managing hirsutism in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.[1]
No studies found on spray formats specifically. A 2021 Cochrane review of 25 studies (8,919 participants) compared razors, clippers, hair-removal cream and no removal before surgery.[2]

timeline.event: Cochrane review of 25 studies compares razors, clippers and depilatory cream before surgery.[2]
